speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of very urgent necessity. It appears now that the rumours projecting a takeover of Gulf Canada by the Canadian National Railways Pension Trust Fund are closer to the truth than ever thought before. That this House instructs the Minister of Transport to launch an immediate investigation into CNR's plans to purchase Gulf Canada Ltd. and also that he investigate the financial relationship between the CNR pension trust fund and CN's investment practices.

subsubtopic: WEST COAST CHINOOK SALMON STOCKS-NEGOTIATIONS WITH UNITED STATES AUTHORITIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is addressed to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, if he can take his place promptly.
The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans is well aware of the seriously devastated state of chinook salmon stocks on the west coast, and he is also aware that in the last year or two the United States commercial and native fishery have taken an increasing toll of Canadian waters-bound chinook salmon by interception at Point Roberts in the Puget Sound area. It is estimated that the U.S. fishermen are taking almost 20 per cent of the total returning chinook stocks and that they are intercepting some 200,000 chinook salmon, while the Fraser River gillnet fishermen last year caught only 20,000 chinook salmon.
I want to ask the minister what progress he has made, either privately or publicly, in obtaining some concessions from the Americans, and from his counterparts in Washington state in particular, to ensure that the U.S. fishery will back off from the Canadian chinook salmon resource.

Is the minister prepared to rescind the closure of the upper part of the Fraser River known as area 29 D and to allow the Fraser River gillnet fishermen, who have been making strong representations to him this week, at least one day's opening a week, bearing in mind that last year the Canadian fishermen had only nine days' fishing while their U.S. counterparts had at least 63 days' fishing on the same Canadian salmon stocks?

speechtext:

Is the minister now prepared to enact the chief recommendation of the National Council of Welfare report, that the child exemption contained in the income tax return be replaced by a much richer child tax credit? speechtext:
1.	Did the government transfer to Indian bands in the province of Saskatchewan, the land that it promised to transfer in the original treaties in the province of Saskatchewan that were signed in 1870 and, if so, how much land (a) was transferred (b) remains to be transferred and on what date will the government complete such transfers?
2.	Does the government recognize the difference between a person who is a treaty Indian (a person with a direct blood relationship to a headman who signed on behalf of an Indian band a treaty) and a person who is a status Indian as a result of being declared a status Indian under the provisions of the Indian Act?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: TRANSFER OF SASKATCHEWAN LAND TO INDIAN BANDS
speechtext:
1.	(a) Treaties 2, 4, 5, 6, 8 and 10 were signed with Indians in Saskatchewan between the years 1871 and 1906. Under these treaties, 68 Saskatchewan bands had approximately 1.7 million acres set aside for their use and benefit.
(b) Validated claims submitted to the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development indicate that approximately 1 million acres more will be set aside as reserve land to satisfy the treaty entitlement of some 20 bands.
The completion of negotiations with Saskatchewan bands over their treaty entitlement will depend largely upon the timetable followed by the Federation of Saskatchewan Indians for the submission of any outstanding claims.
Under the 1930 transfer of natural resources agreements, Crown lands were turned over to the provinces subject to, among other things, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, making sufficient Crown land available to Canada to fulfil the land provisions of treaties. Consequently, although the treaties are with the federal government, Canada must rely on the co-operation of the provinces to make these lands available when needed. Negotiations are under way in Saskatchewan
and every effort is being made to ensure that treaty obligations will be met.
2.	Status Indian is a term that is used synonymously with the term registered Indian. A registered Indian is a person who is entitled to be registered as an Indian in accordance with the Indian Act and who has been recorded as an Indian in the Indian Register.
A large number of status Indians are also treaty Indians. A treaty Indian is a person who is registered as a member of a band that was a signatory to a treaty with the Government of Canada. As a treaty Indian, a person is entitled to the same rights and benefits available to status Indians as weil as to such special benefits as were conferred by the particular treaty his band signed.
3.	The government does consider that there is a difference between a status Indian and a treaty Indian. A status Indian is a person who is registered as an Indian in accordance with the Indian Act. A treaty Indian is a person who is registered as an Indian in accordance with the Indian Act and who is registered as a member of a band that was a signatory to a treaty with the Government of Canada.
4.	The Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development's relationship is with individual Indians and bands as defined under the terms of the Indian Act of 1951. The department, as a matter of policy, has specific contribution arrangements with associations of Indian bands to support consultation with Indians, on issues of policy, for program development and research.
The Queen Victoria Treaty Protective Association (or the Victorian Embassy) claims to represent Indian bands who already have direct access to government or are members of existing Indian associations. Furthermore, the protective association claims an interest in the "Treaty Trust Fund" of which this department has no record. Trust funds are maintained for individual Indian bands rather than on the basis of treaties.

speechtext: The House resumed, from Wednesday, April 8, consideration of Bill C-42, an act to establish the Canada Post Corporation, to repeal the Post Office Act and other related acts and to make related amendments to other acts, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates, and motion No. 9-Mr. Blenkarn (p. 9094).

Madam Speaker, my intervention in support of motion No. 9 to amend Bill C-42 is with respect to the changes of a rather slight nature that the hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) seeks to make to Clause 31 as it presently stands in the bill. Those changes are very brief, but my reason for supporting the proposed amendment goes beyond brevity.
The present provisions of Clause 31 provide for the appointment of dual auditors to act as auditors for the new postal corporation, and the purpose of the amendment is to insert in place of that dual appointment, with the other qualifications that are placed thereon in Clause 31, the Auditor General.
1 had an opportunity earlier today to attend a meeting of the steering committee of the Standing Committee on Public Accounts to discuss with the Auditor General not only this matter but also other matters related to his appointment as auditor for certain Crown corporations. The Auditor General indicated to me and other members of that steering committee of the Standing Committee on Public Accounts that he has corresponded with the Postmaster General (Mr. Ouellet), drawing to the attention of the Postmaster General the unfortunate consequences, as he views them, that will follow his removal as auditor for the current Canada Post Office, upon the incorporation of the Canada Post Corporation, and the replacement of himself by independent auditors.
There has been a tendency of late-a regrettable one-of replacing the Auditor General with outside auditors. The most recent illustration of this development occurred in connection with the intended replacement at the annual meeting of Eldorado Nuclear, to be held on the twenty-eighth day of this month, of the Auditor General by independent auditors.
April 9, 1981

The newly appointed Auditor General, Mr. Kenneth Dye, is carrying on in the fine tradition, well known to this House, of Mr. J. J. Macdonell, as servant of the public who departed from a general tendency of former auditors general by establishing systems to avoid the calamitous results of bad business management in government departments.
We are all well aware of the comprehensive audit system which had been established by Mr. Macdonell and which, from every indication 1 can obtain, is to be continued under the office of the new Auditor General. The concept of the comprehensive audit is not something to be speedily overlooked. It is an extension beyond the attest audit carried out by auditors in the private sector so that Parliament may be advised whether the actions of government departments and Crown corporations audited by the Auditor General meet the tests of economy, efficiency and effectiveness in terms of expenditures.
With respect to Eldorado Nuclear, the Standing Committee on Public Accounts recommended, in fact, that that Crown corporation be subject to just such a comprehensive audit. It would be regrettable if the post corporation, which up until now has been reaching into the consolidated revenue fund on an annual basis for hundreds of millions of dollars in funding in order that it may carry on its activities, will now be replaced by a Crown corporation which, if we pay close attention to the budget of October 28 of last year, will result in a substantial increase in postal fees.
It has been my position that it does not matter whether the public is obliged to pay, through its taxes, for the sustaining of this monolithic monster which has been created or whether as a result of the laws passed by Parliament a corporation be given a monopoly to reach into the pockets of the general public and therefrom extract, through postage rates, the fees necessary for the Crown corporation to carry on its business. I submit that this Parliament has an obligation to the public, and that obligation is to see, through the work of the Auditor General, that public funds derived either, as in the past, by way of direct taxation or, as in the future, by way of obligatory charges for monopolistic services are spent while meeting the tests of economy, efficiency and effectiveness.
The comprehensive audit concept developed by the office of the Auditor General is not extensively known in the private sector, and my great fear is that that type of audit will never be undertaken with respect to this new Crown corporation. It is accordingly, I submit, of vital importance to this House that the Auditor General be retained as auditor for the successor of the Canada Post Office.
Mr. Dye did not depart from his observations in connection with Clause 31 after dealing with the need to reappoint his office but, rather, I understand, in corresponding with the Postmaster General, pointed out that it is not cost-effective to appoint joint auditors. Having recently come from private practice, I understand Mr. Dye has indicated to the Postmaster General-I mention this because although he has spoken on this clause the Postmaster General has not indicated that he is in receipt of the letter to which I made reference-that he
Canada Post Corporation Act
recognizes the dangers of joint appointments. He suggested to the steering committee of the Standing Committee on Public Accounts this morning that two things could occur which are disadvantageous. There is the possibility of an audit gap when two separate firms are dealing with the same set of books, and surely no one wants something missing at the time an audit report is presented. In addition, it is more expensive to have two auditors undertake a task than one, and yet if we examine Clause 31 we find that in fact two auditors are to be appointed.
There is another problem to which the Auditor General has directed his attention, and that is that the short term referred to in Clause 31(1) is unattractive and creates additional cost and expense. That makes good sense. How many public auditing firms have audited the Post Office Department? Very few.
One.

There has only been one, and that is the office of the Auditor General. Does it make sense to pay for the education of a private auditing firm to determine how the Post Office Department will function when converted into a Crown corporation? Does it make any sense to pay for the education of two auditing firms? Of course not. But does it make any sense to perpetuate that educational program by replacing auditors, because of the short term of appointment, every two or three years? The term of appointment, as I have said, under subclause (1) of Clause 31 is for a period of two years only. The answer is that it makes no sense at all. Why would the government wish to incur additional costs to be borne by the users of this service of a kind that is not necessary? It is surely more appropriate, as recommended by the Auditor General, if he is not to be granted the task of supervising the affairs and undertaking the audit of this new Crown corporation, to appoint one outside auditing firm, not two, and let it have a reasonable term of service.
One can only speculate as to the reasons for the determination made by the government, and that is that the government has a number of firms which it would like to reward under a pork-barrel system on a regular rotating basis. That is not in the best interest of the public, nor is in the best interest of the users of the service. It is something that, I submit, Parliament should reject out of hand.
We have heard the comments made by the Postmaster General to the effect that we should be satisfied to await the new Crown corporation legislation which will deal with all the auditing needs and the action to be taken by Auditor General. I have not seen the legislation as it is not before the House, it is not something we can examine, and it is certainly not something we passed. How can we ever say: Let us leave this proposal in its objectionable form and wait for something to happen to clear it up. There is every indication in this House that the objectional form will continue, as is apparent from the fact that today, now that we are so close to this Crown corporation legislation, we are presented with Clause 31 which indicates the very opposite road that the government should be taking. I mentioned earlier with respect to Eldorado Nuclear

April 9, 1981
Canada Post Corporation Act
that under the guise of endeavouring to make changes, the minister responsible for that corporation has given his authority to remove the audit of Eldorado Nuclear from the Auditor General. Are we not in a position to determine what future action the government will probably take with respect to new Crown corporation legislation? I submit we are. The most recent indications are that they will continue a program of reducing the influence and effect of a most faithful servant of the House and of the public.
I should like to comment very briefly on some of the other observations which I understand the Auditor General has made his communique to the Postmaster General. He has indicated that, even as Clause 31 is drafted, it is weak when compared with the obvious requirements for audit-related processes under the Canada Business Corporations Act and under all or most provincial business corporation acts. Surely this large, publicly-owned corporation, in terms of its audit reports and the need for audit committee meetings, should at least meet the general requirements that the federal and provincial governments have insisted should be met by private enterprise, and yet that is not the case. Accordingly, I recommend to the House that motion No. 9 to amend this bill be adopted.

I am not absolutely sure of the procedural situation in which that may put us, but if it is appropriate and if Your Honour rules that I may move this motion in substitution for the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings, and if that is agreed to by the Postmaster General (Mr. Ouellet)-I see him nodding-then I shall proceed.
I will be brief, Mr. Speaker. As all hon. members know, provision is made whereby four householders a year during the fiscal year can be sent to each of our respective ridings. Under the legislation which makes that provision, those four householders have to be sent during the fiscal year. Consequently, hon. members tend to leave the fourth one to the last minute. I see you smiling, Mr. Speaker; I am sure we have all done that. The consequence of that is to create an enormous load for the printing presses and for those officials who assist us in getting our householders to our riding. It also creates a tremendous load on the Post Office facilities all at one time.
The amendment as suggested, which I would like the Postmaster General to consider, is that Clause 34 in the bill be amended to eliminate the words "fiscal year" and replace them with the words "calendar year". The effect of that amendment, it is hoped by my colleague and by the committee which made this recommendation, will be that members will be able to put out four householders during any calendar year, thereby avoiding bottlenecks and the sudden and tremendous increase of activity at the very end of the fiscal year. I think the point is simple; it is a short one. It ought not to be a matter of extended debate. I think I have described the situation succinctly.

speakeroldname: Hon. Andre Ouellet (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Postmaster General) moved:
speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
April 9, 1981
Canada Post Corporation Act
(11)	Where any employees in the Post Office Department are not, immediately before the coming into force of this section, prohibited by the Public Service Staff Relations Act from participating in a strike, the requirements of Subsection 180(1) of the Canada Labour Code are deemed to have been met
in respect of those employees.
68.2 (1) Each employee organization that immediately before the coming into force of this section was certified under the Public Service Staff Relations Act as the bargaining agent for a bargaining unit consisting of or including employees in the Post Office Department is deemed to have been certified as the bargaining agent for the employees of the Corporation in that bargaining unit under Part V of the Canada Labour Code on the day this section comes into force.
(2)	Notwithstanding any provision of Part V of the Canada Labour Code,
(a)	no application for certification as the bargaining agent for any employees of the Corporation represented by a bargaining agent deemed to have been certified under subsection (1) may be made by a trade union, and
(b)	no bargaining unit or part thereof consisting of employees of the Corporation represented by a bargaining agent deemed to have been certified under Subsection (1) may be reviewed, rescinded, amended, altered or varied otherwise than to include in the unit any employees who are not represented by a bargaining agent, before the commencement of the last three months of the first collective agreement entered into after the coming into force of this section that applies to those employees and that has resulted from a notice to bargain collectively given by or to the Corporation after the coming into force of this section.
(3)	For greater certainty, no collective agreement resulting from a notice to bargain collectively deemed to have been given under Subsection 68.1(4) and no arbitral award or collective agreement referred to in Subsection 68.1(7) is a first collective agreement within the meaning and for the purposes of Subsection (2)."
He said: Mr. Speaker, when Bill C-42 was introduced for the first time, Clause 66 was then the first step toward the quiet and orderly transition of a collective bargaining process, that is to say instead of coming under the Public Service Staff Relations Act the collective bargaining process would come under the Canada Labour Code.
While discussions with spokesmen for the Canadian Labour Congress and the major unions of postal workers were continuing, Clause 66 of this first Bill C-42 set forth the basis of the transition by establishing, among other things, the continuation of existing collective agreements, the settlement of outstanding grievances, and the maintenance of the certification of bargaining agents previously certified under the Public Service Staff Relations Act.
I must say, Mr. Speaker, that as a result of those discussions which went on long after second reading and the proceedings of the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates which involved the Department of Labour, the Treasury Board, the Public Service Staff Relations Board, the representatives of the Canadian Labour Congress and of all Canadian postal unions, it was agreed to make further changes which have now been incorporated in the revised and longer version of the new Clause 68 of Bill C-42 which is now before the House.
In fact, Clause 68 contains three quite specific parts: Clause 68, Clause 68.1 and Clause 68.2 which actually govern first, collective agreements now in force, second, collective agreements which have expired, and third, the certification of bargaining agents. I must say that the main difference between Clause 66 of the original bill and the present Clause 68 resides in Clause 68.1. That part is long and complex, and that is why you were dispensed, Mr. Speaker, from reading it all.
It should be kept in mind that postal workers belong to no fewer than eight employees' organizations and are governed by 28 different collective agreements. So at some time, some of those agreements will expire, which will raise some doubt as to the status of the parties. Consequently, we have added a special clause governing collective agreements which will have expired when this legislation will be proclaimed, and it is Clause 68.1 now before you.
These steps are taken especially in cases where the parties are involved in bargaining, arbitration or conciliation, so as to ensure that all procedures in progress are conducted in an orderly fashion. For instance, when the parties are bargaining at the time Subclauses (l)(c), (4) and (5) of Clause 68.1 come into force, the bargaining notice is deemed to have been given; then, the parties agree that Part V of our Labour Code should apply so as to allow the bargaining to proceed without interruption.
In my opinion, it is important to allow this bargaining started in good faith by the representatives of both the employees and the employer to proceed. The bargaining should not have to start all over again from the beginning. The parties should be allowed to continue, which would not have been possible under the original bill. We propose such provisions to make it possible for the arbitration or conciliation in progress to proceed under the Public Service Staff Relations Act, which would not have been possible either under Clause 66 but is now possible under Subclauses (6), (7) and (8) of Clause 68.1.
Thus, Mr. Speaker, we think we can ensure continuity and stability in the early days of the corporation. I point out to you and to all members of the House that this amendment has been discussed with union representatives, with spokesmen for the opposition parties, and especially with the official critic of the New Democratic Party for postal matters, the hon. member for Kootenay East-Revelstoke (Mr. Parker), as well as my predecessor, the former postmaster general, the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser). And we all agree that this amendment which is what representatives of the unions, all the unions, want should be approved by the House.

Mr. Speaker, the marvellous feature of this place is that, despite what the Postmaster General (Mr. Ouellet) has just said in terms of agreement by spokesmen for all parties with respect to the Post Office, as an individual Member of Parliament I am able to expres my substantial concern about what the motion presently before the House omits to include. I am particularly concerned about the provisions of Clause, as hopefully amended by the minister, 68.1(11) which provides:
April 9, 1981

Where any employees in the Post Office Department are not, immediately before the coming into force of this section, prohibited by the Public Service Staff Relations Act from participating in a strike, the requirements of subsection 180(1) of the Canada Labour Code are deemed to have been met in respect of those employees.
The one great omission in the bill, and now perpetuated by the intended amendment, is that there is no prohibition against strikes in what has become an essential service in Canada, whether that essential service be operated by a government department or this new Crown corporation. I have gone so far, as a consequence of consulting with my constituents, to draft Bill C-251, which would have the effect of prohibiting strikes where the convenience, mobility or economic well-being of the public is affected. As I indicated, 1 did that as a consequence of consulting with my constituents. Of 2,676 responses to the question "Should federal civil servants in essential services be allowed to strike?", 88.15 per cent responded "No".
In the event that this bill is passed, even if it is amended as recommended now by the minister, this essential service and any potential amendments to the Public Service Staff Relations Act will pass out of the control of this House. Parliament will be called back to legislate an end to labour disputes.
I know that the hopes and expectations of the minister and other persons of good will are that this bill will end disputes between management and labour in what is now the Canadian postal service. 1 do not share their enthusiasm for a Utopia to be developed as a consequence of the passage of this legislation. Rather than restrict the areas where conflict between management and labour will exist, we have expanded them. The area of potential conflict is greater with the passage of this legislation than it is now, because under the Canada Labour Code the employees of this new corporation will be able to take issue with the conditions of their employment.
Let me give a specific illustration as it affects my riding, where that kind of complaint will exist. The town of Markham, one of the three towns in York North, received normal service from the Canada Post Office up until November of 1980. At that time a decision was made to move postal sorters from what has been regarded as a small, quasi-rural postal station serving the public to Scarborough. As a result, while it previously took three or four days to receive mail, it now takes eight or nine.
The Postmaster General, as a consequence of the receipt of communications from myself and my constituents, is well aware of this fact. However, the essential problem which resulted from the transfer of these employees to Scarborough is that they have become dissatisfied with the transfer because the Scarborough plant is too noisy. The sorting equipment makes a great racket, and it has the effect, according to personnel at the Scarborough sorting station, of driving those postal sorters who were formerly from Markham away from their jobs. They have simply not reported for work.
Now, that is the situation under the Public Service Staff Relations Act. Under the Canada Labour Code, if they do not like the roar of the machines they will go on strike. That is the kind of practical illustration which I think is essential for this House to understand before it endorses this amendment and
Canada Post Corporation Act
passes this legislation. However, the public demand that the postal service-whether it be carried on by a government department or by a Crown corporation-be carried on efficiently in order to serve them. That will not result from the pasage of this recommended amendment, and it will not result from the passage of the bill itself.
The government has shirked its responsibility, in dealing with an essential element of its required service to the public, of supervising the affairs of government departments and now of supervising the introduction of this piece of legislation. It is regrettable that the Postmaster General has so closed his mind to the practical implications of what happens when a strike occurs in Canada.
I wrote to the Postmaster General on March 13 with respect to a problem referred to me by the Markham Hydro Commission, which was concerned about the delivery of utility bills during a work stoppage. It was also concerned about the general practice which it had adopted of having its employees deliver those accounts to customers. I wrote to the Postmaster General and he wrote back to me by letter dated April 6, 1981, which I received in my office yesterday. Attached to his correspondence was a general reply which he had sent to Mr. D. G. Hugill, the president of the Ontario Municipal Electric Association. On page 2 of that letter to Mr. Hugill the Postmaster General said, in response to a question as to whether a utility's staff could deliver bills during a time of strike:
Neither can I support the inclusion of a provision which would permit contracted delivery during postal strikes. A major objective of the Bill is to establish a new foundation to improve labour relations in the Post Office. Legislating this kind of exemption would clearly undermine that objective.
Earlier in his letter he had said:
You believe there should be additional amendments to either completely exempt utility bills, or at least to exempt them during postal service disruptions. While I understand the arguments you have used in support of the suggested general exemption, I cannot lend my support to it for several reasons.
To be fair to the minister, I will read the reasons:
First of all, as you noted in your letter, utility bills fall within the letter monopoly. Making an exception in the case of your utility obviously would be neither fair to other utilities nor indeed to other major users of the postal service's letter stream.
Of probably even greater importance is that making such an exemption would ignore the fact that with respect to the postal service's letter monopoly, much more than the interests of any particular group of firms or any particular group of customers is involved.
Very clearly, the minister has said that it is impossible for the utilities to deliver their utility bills using their employees.
I believe the minister owes an explanation to this House regarding the comments he made on April 7, which are found in Hansard at page 9047. I have spoken to the minister about this and I am sure he will want to clarify the confusion, if any, that has developed in the minds of those who may have read his response to the question. We were dealing with utility bills and as reported at page 9040 of Hansard, in my address to the House, I said:

April 9, 1981
Canada Post Corporation Act
I have also received a letter from the Markham Hydro Commission drawing to my attention the fact that that commission is, or has been until now, in the regular habit of having its bills delivered by those who read hydro meters. That practice, in the event that this legislation is passed in unamended form, will have to come to an end. They were concerned, of course, as are most people carrying on an active business practice, about the effect upon their operation of a mail stoppage, a strike-
I concluded from an examination of the bill that the delivery of utility bills was the exclusive monopoly of the new corporation. I have so advised my constituent.
As reported at page 9047 of Hansard, the hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) said:
I appreciate that, Mr. Speaker, but I think we should try to straighten out this particular issue. Is it the intention of the minister to allow a utility company to employ its own employees to deliver its invoices?
In reply to that question, the minister said:
Mr. Speaker, I am not here to tell the utility companies what to do, nor am I in a position to tell them how to deliver their invoices. They could follow a number of routes. We have allowed them three specific routes under this legislation. The simplest route for them to take is to use the Post Office, and it is the cheapest and best way. If they want to use private couriers to do their deliveries they will have to pay a price for doing it this way. If they want to use their own employees, that is another way of doing it. I am not here to tell them which way they should take. I am just here to say that the easiest way is obviously to use the Post Office.
It is very clear to me that the minister has indicated that there are three ways authorized under Bill C-42 for the utilities to attend to the delivery of their accounts. One of them includes the delivery of those accounts by their own employees. I was about to despatch a copy of that page of Hansard to my constituent and say to him that, regardless of what my view of the law may be, after reading Bill C-42 the minister seems to have a different view. That was the case until yesterday, when I received a letter from the Postmaster General in which he says very clearly that you cannot, as a utility, have your employees deliver your bills, and you cannot do it even if there is a postal strike.
I think it is time the House paused and thought about what it is doing with this piece of legislation. Many people will wake up and discover they are breaking the law, a law that is passed, not by Parliament, but by the Crown corporation under the regulations which it is authorized to pass at its own whim. And in the event the governor in council does not, within 60 days, reject a regulation passed by the Crown corporation, that regulation will be part of the law of Canada. That regulation is the one which will define specifically the word "letter", which is left to the discretion of the Crown corporation. In this regard, I am referring to the provisions of Clause 17(1 )(a) as affected by Clause 17(7) of the draft bill.
In my view, the suggested amendment of the Postmaster General does not deal with the essential issue that is faced by the public of Canada, namely, whether or not we will have dependable postal service upon which the public can rely at all times without fear of an interruption in that service by a strike. Then not only will the business of Canada be carried on, but also individuals who rely upon the postal service will be able to communicate with whomever they choose.

Mr. Speaker, I have a few comments that I wish to make. However, I will not respond to some of the remarks made by the hon. member for York North (Mr. Gamble). I think he made his views very clear at committee stage and he has put them forward again here in the House. His views and mine differ very substantially but I will not comment on that.
I do want to comment on the amendment. I want to pay particular attention to the groups who came forward and helped assist in preparing this complicated amendment. There are some changes which had to be made in order to make legal changes in contracts which have already been signed and those which could possibly be coming up later on in the phasing out of programs.
Because of the co-operation of the various unions involved, of many of the Conservative members, of the Postmaster General (Mr. Ouellet) and his department, everyone was able to sit down and talk. The postal workers came to the committee not as a split group, but as one group under the chairmanship of Shirley Carr of the CLC. They presented their problems and their ideas. Many were accepted but also many were rejected. The Postmaster General in his role as minister listened to them. He presented the ideas and problems to his various groups and returned to the committee. When we were not able to complete the work during committee stage because it was so complicated, the Postmaster General said, "We know the intent of the proposals we are working on; let us iron them out. We will come back to you, and if they are satisfactory we will try to implement these programs." The Postmaster General has done that. He has done it not only to the satisfaction of our party but I believe also to the satisfaction of the critic of the Conservative Party, the CLC and the five unions involved. Now let us get on with the job of putting the amendment into place. We support this amendment and we congratulate everyone involved in bringing this amendment forward.

Mr. Speaker, I will not hold forth very long. However, I want to say that I consider it essential that some definitive legislation be in place so there is not a sudden stoppage of all bargaining and negotiation. It is essential that a number of revisions be made to the act. I have been a union member all of my working life. I believe in the united action of people, particularly when employers are arrogant and will not reason. I come from a union family. For many years my brothers were strong supporters of the United Mine Workers.
As a boy and since, I have gone through a lot of strikes. I do not believe anyone gains from a strike. I remember when we were on strike in the coal mining industry hoping to get a raise. Sometimes we got it, sometimes not. But after everything is over, when you consider the money that has been lost as well as the markets, it is doubtful whether anyone has gained, workers, management or country.
I have spoken to a number of people in the Post Office who feel the same way. The government missed a wonderful oppor-
April 9, 1981

tunity to provide alternatives, not by force or by eliminating the right to strike because that is a right that was gained after many years of sweat and bloodshed, but through bargaining for the workers.
Many people in the Post Office abhor strikes. They feel they gain nothing and build up a mountain of ill-will. The country certainly does not gain from a strike. Some companies go bankrupt and many people are inconvenienced.
It does not appear that any effort has been made to talk to the Post Office about alternatives to striking. Several years ago the Edmonton city police appeared before a committee of which I was a member. They did not want to go on strike. They felt it would give a tremendous advantage to every criminal in the country. However, they needed some means whereby they could get proper treatment, wages and working conditions. They suggested compulsory arbitration.
That was approximately 30 years ago. When I compare their wages and working conditions with those who have gone on strike, I see little difference. If anything, the Edmonton city police are in a superior position. That is the way it should be. The city of Edmonton, representing all the people in Edmonton, should go out of its way to be fair to its employees.
This Crown corporation should set the example for the country by being fair to its employees. The employees should not have to strike for reasonable working conditions and the corporation should not accept conditions that are not fair and reasonable.
The government missed a tremendous opportunity by not going to management and the employees to inform them that it was turning the Post Office into a corporation and would be bringing forward a new act. It could have sought agreement to settle disputes. It might have discussed compulsory arbitration or a labour court, with judges who have a background in labour, who came up the hard way and know what it means to have no bread on their table and see their children go hungry. The workers of this country may be in a mood to come to some agreement, particularly when antagonisms between labour and management are resolved. It is during that phase that it is difficult to get a settlement that will be valuable throughout the years. The Post Office is now going to become a corporation. It is unfortunate that the department has not come up with a better way to settle disputes rather than have workers go on strike. At present, striking is their only weapon. If some alternative were provided, possibly we would see an end to postal strikes which have caused so much havoc in this country.
I want to make one other point before concluding. During a postal strike there should be some mechanism to prevent companies from going broke, people from suffering because their pay cheques do not arrive, troubles that arise when people do not receive insurance policies, for example, and so on. Having gone through three or four terrible postal strikes, we know what they mean. This legislation should be framed to avoid the agony and the difficulties which arise from strikes. Workers in the Post Office do not like the hatred that builds up during a strike. They have to live with it afterwards, and it
Canada Post Corporation Act
is not pleasant. There could have been a tremendous advance in labour relations had there been a will and an attempt to do so. The government has fallen down badly in not providing a means of looking after essential services if and when, God forbid, there is a strike.
There have been many cases where utility bills have been delivered by a group we call the handicapped because they happen to be subnormal. This work gives them an opportunity to earn a living. The hon. member for Brampton-Georgetown (Mr. McDermid) last night talked about boy scouts doing this task. The gas co-operative is a consumers' organization; there is no big money behind it. It is not a giant corporation but gets its money from the pockets of the people. During a strike it has difficulty delivering bills. It is unfortunate that provision is not made to protect essential services.

Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief. I want to make a couple of observations on the motion presented by the Postmaster General (Mr. Ouel-let). I am in agreement with the amendment the Postmaster General has put forward. I know that this amendment is the consequence of long deliberations between the Postmaster General, management of the Post Office and union members who make up the Post Office family. As a consequence we have before us an amendment which incorporates, in as cooperative a form as possible, deliberations which commenced many months ago and which were brought to the forefront while the bill was in committee. As a consequence of further discussions, this amendment has been brought forward by the Postmaster General. It will be supported by my party.
My friend the hon. member for York North (Mr. Gamble) has expressed a point of view which he has also expressed on other occasions. His views about the consequences to the public of work stoppages in the Post Office are legitimate in so far as he and many members of the Canadian public are concerned.
I had a short experience as postmaster general but I have also had nearly four years as opposition critic on labour matters. I do not think we should move to the outright abolition of the right to strike. As the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) said, in economic battles the right to strike is the final defence or weapon, if you like, of workers in any industrial enterprise. To a very real degree the Post Office is an industrial enterprise.
I join with others who search for a better way to settle matters than having strikes in certain areas visited upon the public. Our party had proposed the establishment of a public interest disputes commission with variations on the theme set out some years ago by the Woods Royal Commission which studied industrial disputes in Canada. This is not the time to go into that matter, however.
I want to assure the Postmaster General that he will have the support of this party. We respect the right of our colleague, the hon. member for York North, to answer the call of

April 9, 1981
Canada Post Corporation Act
his conscience and vote according to his convictions in this matter. 1 think the Parliament of Canada is a big enough place that it can put up with differences. While I think I have always been a good party team player, I have often stated publicly, and I state again, that the rigidity of party lines in this House has often done a lot more damage than good.
We will support the amendment. My good friend the hon. member for York North will vote according to his conscience. I think he will probably be representing the opinion of a number of Canadians, but that is his right and I for one respect it.

subsubtopic: PROMOTION OF CLOSER COMMERCIAL AND CULTURAL RELATIONS WITH CARIBBEAN COUNTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want at the outset to express my appreciation to those on the other side of the chamber who after many years have seen fit to pay that tribute to the Caribbean islands and nations which they so richly deserve.
When I first introduced a motion of this nature a few years ago, the nations of central Latin America and parts of South America were not in the turmoil they are in today. Even today few North Americans recognize the great potential the Caribbean and its people have for us in terms of trade and the value of its cultural history.
Today there are about a quarter of a million people from the Caribbean in and around the city of Toronto. Canadian investment in that part of the world is some $400 million. There is in excess of $200 million in trade with that part of the world.
It is an area which stretches from the Panama Canal northeast to the Bahamas, up to Bermuda, south to Trinidad and even further into Guyana and Belize in Latin America. We are talking about ten independent countries. Antigua within the year will become the eleventh. We are talking about the associated states of St. Kitts and Nevis. In addition there are five dependent territories.

April 9, 1981
Canada-Caribbean Relations
This whole area is of tremendous importance to Canadians and to me as an Atlantic Canadian. Our history with the Commonwealth Caribbean nations predates their becoming members of the Commonwealth. Long before Canada was a confederation we traded the usual basic staples from our part of the world, such as fish and lumber, for sugar, molasses and beautiful rum, among other things. However, that was a long time ago.
I mentioned the value of trade with these nations and the value of Canadian investment. That trade and investment is rapidly developing. My concern and that of my distinguished friend and former colleague, Senator Macquarrie, is that in the midst of the turmoil that has developed in that part of the world in recent years, North Americans have, to a degree that I find not acceptable, tended to turn their backs on them. From time to time we disagree with the philosophies of their governments and, indeed, it is fitting that we should. When countries fail to consult their people in the usual way through elections, of course we should express concern, but we should not turn that into a rejection of the people themselves. It is the people for whom we must continue to show concern.
The presence of Cuba, which as we all know is under the influence of Russia, is being felt more and more each day in this troubled area. It is only when nations such as Canada demonstrate that there is another and better way that we can provide the option that the people in these islands need if they are not to fall under the influence of the eastern orbit.
My interest in this matter is somewhat historical, Mr. Speaker. Atlantic Canadians have always had an attachment to that part of the world. There are some concrete things that we should do which have been evident to people from Canada who travel to these islands. Many people go for rest and recreation and usually see only the better or nicer islands. They do not see the privation, the poverty and extreme difficulties that affect many of the people but, they do notice that there is a tangible need for trade and for the facilities to support it.
The motion that I have put before the House calls, in part, for better ports and for the creation of a Canadian merchant marine to facilitate in the further development of trade between our country and these nations. We should not only upgrade our own seaports for this purpose but also those of the receiving countries. It would not be a large undertaking and it is one that would pay enormous dividends to a nation such as ours.
We also need to do more in the areas of health and education. Barbados is one of the key, stable areas of the Commonwealth Caribbean, yet it has only two practising public psychiatrists. I learned recently that there are about 100 psychiatrists in Manitoba, yet that province feels there is a shortage. I am speaking now of a population of between one and two million people which shares two or three psychiatrists. It is an area in which with a little bit of will, Canadians could
make a tremendous contribution to the mental well-being of a lot of people.
There are also other areas that we must consider. Those set forth in my motion barely scratch the surface of the work that must be done. One of the areas in which we could do much more than we are at present-and I have included it because it grows in importance year after year-is in the promotion of the exchange of business people, political leaders, doctors, lawyers, engineers and other technicians. Much could be gained from this. Seminars have been held on progress with respect to program management in the construction industry and these have been very successful. The cost is not great and there should be eight or ten such programs going on in this area.
1 recently visited a new school in one of the Commonwealth Caribbean nations. It had a beautiful library but no books. There was a good home economics classroom with two good gas stoves, but there was no money to buy the tanks of gas needed to start the stoves in order to teach the students to cook. That is the kind of aid that we offer. We frequently put something in place, then say we have done all we can and leave it at that. We can find dozens of instances of our good intentions throughout the Caribbean where we have commenced projects but never really got them off the ground. There is a cocoa replantation project in Granada which was approved almost seven years ago. Not a tree has been planted yet although the program has been approved. It takes 75 years for a cocoa tree to mature, but it will be 75 years before we put the first one in the ground at the rate we are going.
Much of this is the fault of CIDA, although some of it can be overcome, Mr. Speaker. It is hoped that within the next few months, and even beyond that, through the work of the special subcommittee of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence an impetus will be provided for this work and that we will have a constant reminder that we must do more.
The Commonwealth Caribbean has always been important to us and it always will be. It is incumbent upon us to recognize the urgency of the problems that face the people in the Caribbean basin and in Latin and South America.
I appreciate the government's agreement to allow the subject matter of this and one other private motion to go to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence. After taking into consideration the ideas and thoughts presented by members from all sides of this House, I hope that the subcommittee will be able to present to us a full and detailed report on the present status of the relationship between Canada and that part of the world. I hope these motions do not die on the Order Paper, like other subject matters of private members' motions, before the government takes some action on the recommendations which I know will be forthcoming.
April 9, 1981

subsubtopic: PROMOTION OF CLOSER COMMERCIAL AND CULTURAL RELATIONS WITH CARIBBEAN COUNTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion before the House reads as follows:
That a Special Joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons be appointed to consider the advisability of taking an initiative in seeking to promote closer relations with the former British possessions in the West Indies, such as the Turks and Caicos Islands, which have not yet attained independence, and further that if the residents of any of these islands so desire it, economic and political union of these islands with Canada be negotiated at an early date at the proper constitutional levels.
This motion stems from a request made a number of years ago already by the authorities of those islands, according to which they apparently had the intention once of proposing that they become a Canadian protectorate or territory. In the few minutes at my disposal, Mr. Speaker, I will comment briefly on the major aspects of the motion. First, I will talk about the geographical location of those islands. The Turks and Caicos Islands are British possessions located southeast of the Bahamas. Although they are not politically affiliated with the Bahamas they are physically part of those islands. They cover about 175 square miles and have a population of roughly 7,800 inhabitants, mostly blacks.
Several motions were introduced in the House over the years by the opposition parties, mainly the New Democratic Party, with the support of the Progressive Conservatives. On every occasion those motions were rejected by the government on the grounds that they might lead to an upset of the balance in the standard of living between those islands, not to mention complications in immigration procedures, something over which Canada might find it difficult to exercise control. As well, the then external affairs secretary of state equated that possibility with some form of colonialism. I believe the situation has changed appreciably since then, and that is why I suggest there would be major advantages in making an in-depth review of the feasibility and the possibility of a rapprochement between the Turks and Caicos Islands and annexation with either a province of Canada or Canada itself.
Now as far as advantages and disadvantages are concerned, Mr. Speaker we could discuss them at length. However, I expect and hope that the motion will be referred to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence and we would then have the opportunity to deal with them in depth. In the few minutes left to me, Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out that I am convinced that those who get acquainted with that motion will realize the mutual advantages of such a rapprochement. If we solely consider the tourist industry, Mr. Speaker, our adverse trade balance, I refer now to the Economic Review, a Perspective on the Decade, April 1980, Department of Finance and on page 104 I read the following: This deficit and I quote:
-reached a high of $ 1.7 billion in 1978.
Canada-Caribbean Relations
And the trade deficit for the tourist industry -$0.9 billion of which was with the United States.
It means, Mr. Speaker, that in the tourism sector alone, it would be advisable for Canada to at least assess a prospective union with those islands.
From the standpoint of trade, this would lead, of course, to a fairly spectacular development, involving a considerable amount of supplies coming from Canada, a considerable work force from all areas of the building and catering industries. We know we have a lot of know-how in those areas in Canada. Now, I feel that taking into account, for instance, the number of Canadians who go south during the winter months, besides some of our retired people, if it were possible to spend winter holidays in Canada, in a Canadian province, with the same currency, there is good reason for the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence to have a close look at the very least, at the possibility of developing closer ties with those islands. I have barely touched upon some of the advantages-I am sure some will say some disadvantages could also be mentioned-but times have changed since those motions on closer ties were brought foward in the House and 1 think that with regard, for example, to immigration, there should be no problems of any consequence in view of the efficiency of the controls implemented today. As for the imbalance it might create with the other islands, there again I doubt that the argument is valid. As far as colonialism is concerned, which was brought up at the time, once again, if we come to an agreement that is mutually satisfactory, I fail to see how that could be interpreted as colonialism. Both sides would, I think, derive considerable advantages from such an agreement and that is why I have great hope that this House will agree, at least, to referring this motion to the standing committee.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I say-which I am sure is no news to you-that Canada is the greatest country in the world in every regard. It could actually be a true Garden of Eden but for one thing: a place we can call home, where we can visit and rest, basking in a tropical clime. For all those reasons, I hope the House will accept my motion.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subsubtopic: PROMOTION OF CLOSER COMMERCIAL AND CULTURAL RELATIONS WITH CARIBBEAN COUNTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to offer my congratulations to the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) and the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Tousignant) on the two resolutions they have placed before the House today. I should also like to congratulate the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Collenette) for making the necessary arrangements so that we can discuss both of these resolutions at the same time. I hope I am not jumping the gun if I also thank him for the motion which he will probably make a little later that the subject matter of the two resolutions be referred to the appropriate committee for study.

April 9, 1981
Canada-Caribbean Relations
The subject matter of these motions has long been the interest of quite a few people in the Canadian Parliament and I think it is time we gave very close study to the possibility of developing closer relations with the peoples of the Caribbean nations.
I have mentioned the two members who have placed the motions before us today. I think we should also recall the efforts, especially regarding the Turks and Caicos Islands, which were made session after session by a former colleague of mine, Mr. Max Saltsman, who came here as the member for Waterloo South, which was later called Waterloo-Cambridge. I am also conscious of the keen interest in the Caribbean of the former member for Hillsborough, now Senator Heath Mac-quarrie. We do have these interests as part of the record, and I hope we will build thereon and give serious study to ways in which we might make our relations closer.
Many of us in this House have had the pleasure of visting the Caribbean. The two islands 1 have had the pleasure of visiting are Jamaica and Trinidad. I know the name of the country is Trinidad and Tobago but my visit was on the island of Trinidad. In mentioning that country, I think we might express in this House our regret at the recent untimely death of Dr. Eric Williams, the prime minister of Trinidad and Tobago, who did such a good job of achieving stability in a part of the world where there is a fair amount of instability.
Those of us who have been down there know that the feeling there toward Canada and Canadians is very warm, and 1 think it would be good for them and good for us if we had closer relations.
I have mentioned-I know it is a bit personal but it is in my mind-visiting both Jamaica and Trinidad. I can say that persons from these two islands have rendered me and my family a much appreciated service in my own home in Winnipeg, and I am happy to say that a number of these people, all black or brown, call me Grandpa which I like very much.
So I am grateful to the parliamentary secretary for the motion which I believe he will move, and I trust the House will approve it so there can be further study of this important and very human subject.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. M. Collenette (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: PROMOTION OF CLOSER COMMERCIAL AND CULTURAL RELATIONS WITH CARIBBEAN COUNTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) and the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Tousignant) for bringing these two motions to the House for study, and I am particularly grateful for the co-operation I received from the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East who rushed back from his official visit Jo Italy and immediately after touching down before five o'clock came down here. 1 am sure he is quite exhausted, but certainly, with dedication such as this, I think the House would do him justice in seeing that the subject matter of the motion is referred to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence.
My colleague, the hon. member for Temiscamingue, put a particularly good motion before us, one that was the subject of comment. It is a motion which has been put before the House
by the former member for Waterloo-Cambridge, Mr. Saltsman of the NDP, and which was debated for many years. I am speaking now as a private member, not in my capacity as parliamentary secretary, when I say that I could not understand why the government did not pursue the motion more fully by exploring links with the Turks and Caicos Islands. I think one of the particular problems may have been, as I discovered, having talked with representatives of the Turks and Caicos Islands at some conferences of the parliamentary association, that if there were ever to be such a union with Canada they would want some kind of special status and perhaps would not be willing to join on the same basis as did other provinces such as Newfoundland, when it came into confederation, or Alberta and Saskatchewan in 1905. Perhaps that may be the sticking point. However, it is an idea which should be pursued and I hope this is the first step in the pursuit of that idea.
The other reason I am particularly glad to be representing the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) here this evening is that in my constituency I have many people from the West Indies. Our Commonwealth Caribbean friends have made a distinct contribution, not only to my constituency but to the life of metropolitan Toronto. Indeed, some of my greatest friends are people who originally came from the West Indies. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) reminisced about his personal visits to the West Indies. I think there are very few Canadians who have not visited at least one Caribbean island.
A couple of years ago I went to the conference of the Commonwealth parliamentary association held in Port of Spain, Trinidad, and I also visited Barbados on a holiday a few years ago. I concur in the sentiments expressed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre about the affection and closeness with which people from those islands regard Canada and the distinct and unique bond between us which makes it even more appropriate that we discuss the subject here this evening.
I should say in delivering some official remarks on behalf of the Secretary of State for External Affairs that I will be proposing a motion that the subject matter of these two motions be referred to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence. Hon. members may ask why we are not referring the motions themselves, and perhaps I could take a minute to explain that. This is said with no disrespect to the two members proposing the motions.
There are five areas listed in the motion of the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East, one being subsidization of seaborne transport between Canada and the Commonwealth Caribbean area, another being the assistance in the upgrading of the seaports of Atlantic Canada, and three others. They are something on which the government does not necessarily wish to commit itself at this stage, and I would even venture to say that had the motion stopped after the words "Commonwealth Caribbean", we would probably be approving this motion unanimously. However, I think it bears further study, both by the government and the committee, as to whether or not the
April 9, 1981

areas listed in the motion of the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East are areas which should be emphasized.
Motion No. 36 in the name of the hon. member for Temis-camingue is also, I believe, a worthy one, but the reason we are only referring the subject matter to the committee is again that the motion itself goes into a few specifics on which the government is not prepared to commit itself. It may be that after discussion in committee, a report will come back on these two subjects and there may be concurrence in the House. We will then have achieved something of some substance for the two hon. members who have brought the motions before us.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs has asked me to present some general remarks on the subject. In particular, he wants me to acknowledge the fact that the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence has already received a reference to examine Canada's relationship with Latin America and the Caribbean. The committee's current investigations and both of these motions reflect, in the government's view, the continuing and growing interest of the government and people of Canada in our relations with our neighbours in the western hemisphere, in particular with the Commonwealth Caribbean.
As Mr. Speaker knows from his travels with various Commonwealth Parliamentary Association delegations, the Canadian government has been an active participant in the economic development of the Commonwealth Caribbean for a quarter of a century. I see the hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) is present in the House. He is the past president of the Canadian branch of the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association; I know of his great interest and work in this particular area.
In the autumn of 1956, when the notion of a federation of English-speaking island states of the region was in the air, the then Canadian Secretary of State for External Affairs, Lester Pearson, convened a conference of Caribbean leaders in Ottawa, during which the first significant pledge of Canadian official assistance was made to the then embryonic University of the West Indies. This university was to formulate the beginning of the Caribbean Broadcasting Corporation.
A decade later, in 1966, the Hon. Paul Martin, another distinguished former Secretary of State for External Affairs, a former High Commissioner and senator, chaired a second Commonwealth Caribbean conference in Ottawa, during the course of which Canada renewed its pledge to assist the states of the Commonwealth Caribbean on a continuing basis.
Over the 15 years since the second Ottawa conference on the Caribbean, the Canadian Development Assistance Program to the region-bilateral, multilateral, non-government organizational, industrial co-operation, grant and loan, direct and indirect-has been put in place to quicken economic growth in the Caribbean, leading naturally and inevitably to a redefinition of the Canada-Commonwealth Caribbean relationship.
Canada-Caribbean Relations
Two years ago in Kingston, Jamaica, the then Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Hon. Don Jamieson, was proud to sign for Canada the agreement with CARICOM, otherwise known as the Caribbean Community and Common Market, on trade and economic co-operation. It was the first formal meeting at ministerial level between CARICOM and Canada. Initial progress in providing substance to the trade, technical, financial and industrial co-operation provisions of the 1979 agreement has been modest, but solid and real.
Essentially our first contacts were exploratory in nature. They were followed by useful work by officials at the November, 1979, Joint Trade and Economic Committee meeting in Ottawa and in the subsequent meeting of the ad hoc committee on industrial co-operation in the Barbados.
There is commitment to a new and dynamic thrust to the CARICOM relationship. In the past year, a comprehensive review of Canada's relations with the Commonwealth Caribbean has been commissioned, completed, considered and approved by cabinet. This review included an examination of Canada-Commonwealth Caribbean trade and investment, Canada-Commonwealth Caribbean people-to-people links, Canada's development co-operation relationship with the Caribbean, and Canada's political links with the Caribbean.
The review took eight months of preparation involving extensive consultations in Ottawa and the full and active participation of the Canadian High Commissioners in the field. The review confirmed, as official policy, that the Commonwealth Caribbean is and will continue to be a region of major interest to Canada.
In fact, the government went beyond the mere provision of an assessment; cabinet approved an action plan for a regional policy approach which directed that the Commonwealth Caribbean should be accorded priority.
The review concluded that Canada should intensify and deepen its economic and political relationships with the states of the Commonwealth Caribbean. The government wants this partnership to assist those states to cope with rapid changes and economic difficulties which beset the region. The regional policy approach which the Canadian government is prepared to implement focuses primarily on economic co-operation, both bilateral and multilateral, but also calls for strengthening of political and social ties.
The present Secretary of State for External Affairs launched the policy in January when he visited the eastern Caribbean and Jamaica and met with Commonwealth Caribbean ministers to seek their views on this regional policy approach.
The second motion reflecting the idea of closer association between Canada and the Turks and Caicos Islands has been the subject of public interest and parliamentary debate for some years. The Turks and Caicos Islands are an economically underdeveloped British colony with minimal but good relations with Canada. The government's position, which was enunciated in 1974, has been that it did not favour discriminating in favour of one state in the region. It was concluded that

April 9, 1981

association would result in Canadians dominating the economy of the islands, raising the possibility of social tensions and accusations of neo-colonialism. This subject remains of interest to Parliament and the people of Canada. Therefore, its examination by the committee is in the minister's view both useful and timely.
In closing, I should like to echo the sentiments of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre who paid tribute to the late Dr. Eric Williams, the prime minister of Trinidad and Tobago for 21 years. Ele was an individual who contributed to the adolescence of the Caribbean community. I am not referring to just his own island; he presided over a great surge in economic growth in his country of Trinidad and Tobago. He was a respected elder statesman in the Caribbean community. We all mourn his passing last week. We hope the Caribbean community, as a whole, will look toward the leadership he has given over the years and perhaps emulate his policies and deep commitment to the people of the Caribbean as part of the model for future action and development.
At this time just before the supper hour, I would like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That motions Nos. 31 and 36, standing in the names of the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East and the hon. member for Temiscamingue, respectively, be withdrawn and that the subject matters thereof be referred to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence.
I hope this motion will be acceptable to hon. members of the House.
